title: Merge Intervals: Insert an Interval
oneLiner: The list is already sorted and non-overlapping, so one O(n) pass splits it into three runs: before the new interval, overlapping it, and after it.
keyTakeaway: Because the intervals are sorted and don't overlap each other, the ones that overlap the new interval form ONE contiguous run. Copy everything that ends before the new interval starts, absorb the run that overlaps it (min of starts, max of ends), then copy the rest. No sort is needed, so it's O(n).
explanation:
You get a list of intervals that is sorted by start and has no overlaps, plus one new interval. Insert the new interval and merge wherever it now overlaps, so the result is again sorted and non-overlapping. Touching endpoints count as overlapping: [1, 2] plus [2, 3] becomes [1, 3]. For [[1, 2], [3, 5], [6, 7], [8, 10], [12, 16]] with new interval [4, 8] the answer is [[1, 2], [3, 10], [12, 16]].

You could append the new interval and run the general merge from Merge Intervals: Combine Everything That Overlaps, but that sorts again, O(n log n), and ignores the fact that the list is already in order. Because the existing intervals are sorted and disjoint, the ones that overlap the new interval sit next to each other. That splits the list into three runs, and one left-to-right pass handles them in order.

First run: while the current interval ENDS before the new one STARTS (end < newStart), it can't touch the new interval, so copy it to the output unchanged. Second run: while the current interval STARTS at or before the new one ENDS (start <= newEnd), it overlaps, so widen the new interval to cover it: newStart = min(newStart, start), newEnd = max(newEnd, end). When that loop stops, append the widened interval. Third run: everything left starts after the widened interval ends, so copy it unchanged. Every interval is looked at once: O(n) time, and O(n) for the output.

The two comparisons decide what "overlap" means. Using end < newStart in the first loop and start <= newEnd in the second treats touching intervals as overlapping, which is what this problem wants. Notice the new interval can swallow many intervals, none, or land before the first or after the last, and the same three loops cover all of those without special cases.

The visualization inserts [4, 8]; the cells show the output as it's built.

recognitionSignals: The intervals are ALREADY sorted and non-overlapping, and one new interval has to be added while keeping that property.
An O(n) bound, or a hint that re-sorting is wasteful, on what would otherwise be a merge-intervals problem.
gotchas: Mixing up which ends to compare: "entirely before" is end < newStart, "overlaps" is start <= newEnd. Swapping them, or using the new interval's ORIGINAL end after it has been widened, drops or double-counts intervals.
Forgetting to append the merged new interval when there was nothing to merge with (empty list, or it fits in a gap or at either end).
Absorbing only ONE overlapping interval with an if instead of a while: the new interval can swallow several, and each one it absorbs can push its end further right.
confusableWith: Merge Intervals (this track) starts from UNSORTED intervals and needs a sort first, O(n log n). Here the input is already sorted and disjoint, so a single O(n) pass is enough; re-sorting works but misses the point.
Binary search can find where the new interval starts in O(log n), but the merged output still has to be built, so the total stays O(n).

complexity.note: One pass: every interval is either copied or absorbed exactly once, and no sort is needed because the input is already sorted. The output list holds up to n + 1 intervals.

referenceSolutions.python:
def insert_interval(intervals, new_interval):
    result = []
    start, end = new_interval
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < start:  # ends before the new one starts
        result.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= end:  # overlaps: absorb it
        start = min(start, intervals[i][0])
        end = max(end, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    result.append([start, end])
    result.extend(intervals[i:])  # everything left starts after the merged one ends
    return result
